commons.title: Gullah s carolina 1790.jpg
commons.description: "The Old Plantation," South Carolina, about 1790. This famous painting shows Gullah slaves dancing and playing musical instruments derived from Africa. Scholars unaware of the Sierra Leone slave trade connection have interpreted the two female figures as performing a "scarf" dance. Sierra Leoneans can easily recognize that they are playing the shegureh, a women's instrument (rattle) characteristic of the Mende and neighboring tribes.
commons.editorial_reason: The caption specifically identifies Gullah enslaved people dancing and playing African-derived instruments, which the image visibly depicts.

commons.title: Sea Island red peas.jpg
commons.description: Sea Island red peas are a cultivar of Vigna unguiculata subsp. Unguiculata. They were brought to the Sea Islands of the American south via the Trans-Atlantic slave trade. This variety of Cowpea is an endemic heirloom of the Gullah people that inhabit the islands.
commons.editorial_reason: Although the description links the peas to Gullah heritage, the image is a generic food close-up without visibly distinctive cultural content.

commons.title: Come By Here Kumbaya Transcription of 1926 recording.jpg
commons.credit: Author unknown. Sung by H Wylie. Recorded by Robert Winslow Gordon. Transcription: Jennifer Cutting.
commons.description: Transcription of a 1926 recording stored at the Library of Congress. The song "Come By Here" is more popularly known as "Kumbaya" or "Kum Ba Ya." The transcription appears to translate the original language.
commons.editorial_reason: The image is sheet music, and neither the caption nor visible content specifically ties it to Gullah culture.

commons.title: Kongo Cosmogram 01.png
commons.description: The Yowa, or Dikenga Cross, is a symbol in Bakongo spirituality that depicts the physical world, the spiritual (ancestral) world, the Kalûnga river (line) that runs between the two worlds, and the four moments of the sun.
commons.editorial_reason: The image is a modern graphic about Bakongo spirituality, concerning another people rather than Gullah culture.
